categories.label: Data & market readiness

categories.label: Operational controls

categories.label: Claims discipline

industries.label: 3PL, warehousing & distribution
industries.description: Third-party logistics, public and contract warehousing, cold chain, fulfillment, and regional distribution.
industries.marketNote: Carriers evaluating warehousing and 3PL accounts look closely at warehouse legal liability, cargo and customer contracts, fleet controls, fire protection, and how consistently incidents are reported.

industries.label: Light manufacturing
industries.description: Fabrication, assembly, food and beverage, plastics, packaging, electronics, and other light industrial operations.
industries.marketNote: Underwriters reviewing manufacturers focus on product liability and recall exposure, machine guarding and workers' compensation history, property valuation, business interruption, and supplier and customer contract terms.

industries.label: Other middle-market business
industries.description: Any other commercial operation. Uses generic weighting.
industries.marketNote: Carriers evaluate every account on the quality of its exposure data, controls, claims history, and the clarity of the story that accompanies the submission.

questions.prompt: When does renewal preparation typically begin relative to your policy expiration?
questions.help: Carriers reward complete submissions delivered early. Late starts compress negotiation time.

options.label: Within 30 days of expiration, or when the broker reaches out
About 60 days out, but it varies year to year
90+ days out with a written timeline
120+ days out with a documented calendar, owners, and a pre-renewal strategy meeting

critical.message: Renewal preparation appears to begin inside 30 days of expiration, which limits the ability to document controls and approach alternative markets.

questions.prompt: Who owns the insurance program internally, and how is that responsibility defined?

options.label: No single owner; whoever the broker contacts handles it
One person handles it informally alongside other duties
A named owner with defined responsibilities
A named owner, a backup, and a cross-functional review (finance, operations, HR/safety)

questions.prompt: How are policy limits and deductibles decided each year?
questions.help: This question asks about your decision process, not whether the limits are adequate.

options.label: We renew the same limits without discussion
The broker recommends and we generally accept
We review limits against contracts, assets, and revenue annually
We document the rationale for each limit and deductible and revisit it when the business changes

questions.prompt: How are exposure values (payroll, revenue, property values, vehicle schedules, inventory) validated before submission?

options.label: We use last year's numbers unless someone flags a change
We update the big items but rarely reconcile schedules
Finance validates values annually against records
Values are reconciled against financials, fixed-asset registers, and schedules, with sign-off before submission

logistics_3pl.help: For a 3PL this includes the value of customers' goods in your care, custody, and control, vehicle and trailer schedules, and square footage by location.

light_manufacturing.help: For a manufacturer this includes machinery and equipment values, a business-interruption worksheet, and any dependence on a single supplier or customer.

questions.prompt: How are operational changes (new services, locations, equipment, customers, headcount) communicated to your insurance program during the year?

options.label: They surface at renewal, if at all
We mention major changes when we remember
A defined process captures changes and shares them with the broker
Changes are logged, reviewed quarterly for insurance impact, and reflected in mid-term endorsements when needed

questions.prompt: How much visibility do you have into what is actually sent to carriers about your company?
questions.help: The underwriting story is the narrative and evidence that accompanies applications and loss runs.

options.label: None; we sign applications and the broker handles the rest
We submit updated information annually but have not seen how our story is told to carriers
We review the submission and know which carriers quoted or declined
We collaborate with our broker on how best to portray the company in the marketplace, review the full submission, and receive a market summary with reasons for declinations

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes your cyber controls (MFA, backups, endpoint protection, incident response)?

options.label: Basic antivirus; MFA and tested backups are not consistently in place
MFA on email; backups exist but are not tested regularly
MFA on email and remote access, tested offline backups, endpoint detection, and a written incident plan
All of the prior plus annual testing, vendor security review, and executive reporting

critical.message: Multi-factor authentication and tested backups do not appear to be consistently in place. Most cyber carriers now treat these as minimum requirements.

questions.prompt: How are changes to vendor bank details and outgoing wire requests verified?

options.label: No formal protocol; an email or phone request is usually sufficient
Some combination of dual authorization and written procedures, applied inconsistently
Written procedure with callback verification to a known number and dual approval for all bank changes and wires
Formal written program with regular training: dual authorization, callback verification, destination confirmation, and receipt confirmation

critical.message: Vendor bank-detail changes and wires may be released on an email or phone request alone, which is the most common path for social-engineering losses.

questions.prompt: How are safety programs, training, and inspections documented?

options.label: Training happens on the job; little is written down
Some written procedures; training records are incomplete
Written safety program, documented training, and periodic inspections
Written program with documented training, inspections, near-miss reporting, and management review of results

logistics_3pl.prompt: How are warehouse and dock safety (forklift certification, racking, housekeeping), fire protection (sprinkler inspections, impairment procedures, commodity storage), and driver training documented?
logistics_3pl.help: Warehouse underwriters look first at fire protection and forklift and dock injury controls.

light_manufacturing.prompt: How are machine guarding, lockout/tagout, hearing and respiratory protection, and safety training documented?
light_manufacturing.help: Machine guarding and lockout/tagout drive both workers' compensation experience and product-safety credibility with underwriters.

questions.prompt: What happens when an incident or potential claim occurs?

options.label: It is reported when someone thinks of it, sometimes weeks later
Supervisors know to report, but timing and format vary
A written protocol defines who reports, how, and within what timeframe
Written protocol, reporting within 24–48 hours, an incident form, and tracking of every report

critical.message: Incidents appear to be reported inconsistently or late. Late reporting is a frequent driver of higher claim costs and coverage disputes.

questions.prompt: How often are open claims and reserves reviewed with your broker or carrier?

options.label: We do not review open claims
Only when the carrier or broker raises something
Scheduled reviews at least twice a year
Quarterly claim reviews with reserve challenges, adjuster accountability, and pre-renewal loss-run reconciliation

questions.prompt: After an incident, how are root causes identified and corrective actions tracked?

options.label: We fix what is obvious and move on
Supervisors discuss causes; actions are not tracked
Root-cause review for significant incidents with documented corrective actions
Every incident gets a root-cause review, corrective actions are tracked to closure, and trends are reported to leadership

questions.prompt: Before work begins with customers, vendors, or subcontractors, how consistently are written contracts in place?

logistics_3pl.prompt: Before goods are received or work begins, how consistently are written warehousing agreements, customer contracts, and carrier/vendor agreements in place?
logistics_3pl.help: Warehouse receipts and customer contracts define your legal liability for goods in your care. Unsigned or inconsistent terms are a common gap.

light_manufacturing.prompt: How consistently are written supply agreements, customer purchase terms, and vendor contracts in place before production or shipment begins?
light_manufacturing.help: Customer terms often carry product warranty, recall, and indemnity obligations that shape your liability program.

options.label: Often work starts on a handshake or PO alone
Contracts exist for major relationships; smaller ones vary
Signed contracts are required before work begins
Signed contracts required, with standard indemnity and insurance language reviewed by counsel and tracked centrally

questions.prompt: How do you determine what insurance to require from the parties you work with, and what they require from you?

logistics_3pl.help: Customers commonly require warehouse legal liability, cargo, and auto limits. Carriers and subcontracted haulers should be held to defined requirements in return.

light_manufacturing.help: Large customers often specify product liability limits and vendor endorsements; suppliers should be held to defined requirements for the components they provide.

options.label: We do not set requirements; we accept whatever the other party proposes
We use a generic requirement list without reviewing it
Requirements are defined by relationship type and reviewed by broker or counsel
Requirements are defined, reviewed annually, and cross-checked against our own policies and customer demands

questions.prompt: How are certificates of insurance and endorsements (additional insured, waiver of subrogation) verified?

options.label: We collect certificates when asked but do not review them
Someone checks that a certificate exists; endorsements are rarely verified
Certificates and required endorsements are verified before work and on expiration
Verification is tracked in a system, endorsements are matched to contract terms, and non-compliance is escalated

critical.message: Certificates of insurance are collected but not reviewed, so contractual risk transfer may not be operating when a loss occurs.

questions.prompt: Does leadership conduct a structured risk review outside of the insurance renewal?
questions.help: A risk review looks at operations, contracts, and controls, not just the policies being renewed.

options.label: Never, or more than five years ago
More than 18 months ago, or only when a new broker or agent first came on board
An annual risk review with a documented risk list
Annual review with owners, action plans, and quarterly progress updates to leadership

questions.prompt: How are regulatory and compliance changes affecting your operations monitored?

options.label: We learn about changes when we are notified of a violation or audit
Individual managers watch their own areas informally
A defined owner monitors regulations and briefs leadership
Defined owner, documented compliance calendar, and periodic compliance audits

questions.prompt: When you add a new location, product, service, technology, or major customer, is risk and insurance impact reviewed beforehand?

logistics_3pl.prompt: When you take on a new commodity, temperature-controlled or hazardous storage, a new customer contract, or a new facility, is risk and insurance impact reviewed beforehand?

light_manufacturing.prompt: When you launch a new product, add a production line or process, or enter a new market, is product liability, recall, and business-interruption impact reviewed beforehand?

options.label: Not usually; insurance catches up later
Sometimes, for very large changes
A review step is included in the launch process
Documented pre-launch review with operations, finance, broker input, and follow-up after launch

questions.prompt: For the buildings you own, how are replacement values, business-interruption values, flood exposure, building updates (roof, sprinklers, electrical), and carrier loss-control recommendations documented and tracked?
questions.help: Carriers issue recommendations after inspections. How you respond to them is part of the underwriting story.

options.label: Values are carried forward; building updates and carrier recommendations are not tracked
Values were reviewed a few years ago; we do the minimum needed to stay compliant with carrier recommendations
Replacement and BI values are reviewed annually; update history and recommendation responses are documented

Professional valuation within three years, BI worksheet, flood zone determination, documented inspections and update history, and an active protocol for responding to and tracking every carrier recommendation

questions.prompt: How are drivers screened and vehicles managed (MVRs, telematics, hired and non-owned auto)?

options.label: We do not run MVRs consistently; personal vehicle use is not addressed
MVRs at hire only; no written fleet policy
Written fleet policy, annual MVRs, and a defined hired/non-owned auto approach
Written policy, annual MVRs with disqualification criteria, telematics or cameras, and driver training records

critical.message: Motor vehicle records do not appear to be run consistently, which commercial auto underwriters treat as a primary control.

questions.prompt: For subcontractors and vendors, how consistently are indemnity terms, additional-insured status, and waivers of subrogation obtained and enforced?

options.label: We rely on the vendor's own paperwork
Our agreement includes the terms, but we rarely confirm the endorsements
Terms are standard and endorsements are confirmed before work
Terms are standard, endorsements confirmed, non-compliant vendors are stopped from working, and exceptions are approved in writing

questions.prompt: For the sensitive customer, employee, or payment data you hold, how are access, vendor security, and incident response managed?

options.label: Access is broad; we have not reviewed vendor security or an incident plan
Access is limited informally; incident response is undocumented
Role-based access, vendor security review, and a written incident response plan
All of the prior plus annual tabletop exercises, data inventory, and breach-notification readiness

questions.prompt: With a workforce of this size, how are workers' compensation return-to-work, employment practices (handbook, training, documentation), and benefits data protection handled?

options.label: No return-to-work program; handbook is outdated or missing
Handbook exists; return-to-work and manager training are informal
Written return-to-work program, current handbook, and documented manager training
All of the prior plus experience-mod review, claims-trend analysis, and annual employment-practices training

questions.prompt: With outside investors or a board, how are directors & officers, fiduciary, and governance-related exposures reviewed?

options.label: They have not been reviewed
Coverage was placed at the time of investment and not revisited
Reviewed annually with the broker against bylaws, investor agreements, and benefit plans
Annual review plus board reporting on limits, indemnification agreements, and fiduciary controls

questions.prompt: For regulated materials or processes, how are environmental permits, storage practices, and pollution exposure managed?

options.label: We are not sure what permits apply; storage practices are informal
Permits are in place; documentation of storage and disposal is inconsistent
Permits, storage, and disposal are documented with a compliance owner
Documented compliance program, periodic environmental audits, and pollution exposure reviewed with the broker

findings.title: Your renewal process may begin too late to fully document your risk controls.
findings.body: Renewal preparation appears to begin with limited runway. Controls that are not documented in time rarely make it into the submission carriers evaluate.
findings.detail: Benchmark indication: high-impact underwriting strengths were identified elsewhere in your answers, but they may not be incorporated consistently into carrier submissions.

findings.title: Your contracts and insurance-verification process may not be operating as one control system.
findings.body: Answers about signed contracts, insurance requirements, and certificate verification are uneven. Risk transfer only works when all three align.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: review whether contractual requirements, certificates of insurance, and policy endorsements align for your largest customer and vendor relationships.

findings.title: Your business has changed faster than your insurance-governance process.
findings.body: You reported recent acquisitions or new locations, but operational changes reach the insurance program late or inconsistently.
findings.detail: Areas to investigate: new locations, increased payroll, new services, and updated property values, and whether each is reflected in current schedules.

findings.title: Your claims process appears reactive rather than managed to a defined cadence.
findings.body: Incident reporting, open-claim review, or corrective-action tracking appear informal. Claims that are not managed tend to cost more and stay open longer.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: evaluate reporting timelines, reserve review, adjuster accountability, and how corrective actions are tracked to closure.

findings.title: Incomplete exposure data or a weak underwriting narrative could limit your market options.
findings.body: Exposure values appear to be carried forward without reconciliation, or you have limited visibility into what carriers receive.
findings.detail: Pricing cannot be assessed from this questionnaire alone. However, carriers generally offer their best terms to accounts that present validated data and a clear narrative, subject to policy, loss, and underwriting review.

findings.title: Payment-change and wire controls may leave a path open for social-engineering losses.
findings.body: Vendor bank-detail changes or wires may be released without callback verification and dual approval. This is the most common route for funds-transfer fraud.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: confirm callback procedures, approval thresholds, and whether crime or cyber coverage includes social-engineering terms, subject to policy review.

findings.title: Cyber controls may not meet the minimums that most carriers now require.
findings.body: Multi-factor authentication, tested backups, and a written incident plan are the controls cyber underwriters ask about first.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: document current controls, close gaps before the next cyber application, and confirm which controls are attested on existing applications.

findings.title: Insurance program ownership appears informal.
findings.body: Without a named owner and defined responsibilities, renewal tasks, certificate requests, and mid-term changes tend to fall through the cracks.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: assign an owner and backup, and define the touchpoints with finance, operations, and HR/safety.

findings.title: Limits and deductibles appear to be renewed without a documented rationale.
findings.body: This diagnostic does not assess whether limits are adequate. It does note that limits which are never revisited may not track contract requirements or asset growth.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: document the basis for each limit and deductible with a licensed advisor and revisit it when contracts or assets change.

findings.title: Safety and training practices may exist but are not documented in a form underwriters can credit.
findings.body: Written programs, training records, and inspection logs are what carriers use to distinguish a well-run operation from an average one.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: assemble a safety documentation package before the next submission.

findings.title: Owned-property values and building updates may be undocumented.
findings.body: Replacement cost, business-interruption values, flood exposure, and building-system updates drive both coverage terms and pricing conversations.
findings.detail: Areas to investigate: date of last valuation, BI worksheet, flood zone determination, and documented roof, sprinkler, and electrical updates.

findings.title: Fleet and driver controls may not be documented to the level auto underwriters expect.
findings.body: MVR practices, fleet policy, and hired/non-owned auto handling are primary controls for commercial auto.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: adopt a written fleet policy with annual MVRs and disqualification criteria.

findings.title: Subcontractor and vendor risk transfer may not be enforced.
findings.body: Indemnity terms and endorsements that are not confirmed before work begins may not respond when a loss occurs.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: confirm additional-insured and waiver endorsements for active vendors.

findings.title: Workforce programs (return-to-work, handbook, manager training) may be informal for a company of your size.
findings.body: These programs influence workers' compensation experience and employment-practices exposure.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: document return-to-work procedures and update the employee handbook.

findings.title: Board and investor-related exposures may not have been reviewed since the investment.
findings.body: Directors & officers, fiduciary, and indemnification arrangements are typically revisited as ownership and boards change.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: review governance-related exposures with a licensed advisor against current bylaws and investor agreements.

findings.title: Environmental compliance and pollution exposure may not be documented.
findings.body: Permits, storage practices, and disposal records are the starting point for any environmental conversation with carriers.
findings.detail: Areas to investigate: applicable permits, storage documentation, and whether pollution exposure has been reviewed.

findings.title: New activities and regulatory changes may reach the insurance program after the fact.
findings.body: Without a pre-launch review step, new locations, products, and technology can create exposures that are not reflected until the next renewal.
findings.detail: Potential opportunity: add a risk and insurance checkpoint to your launch process.

modules.name: MarketReady Risk Diagnostic
modules.headline: How ready is your company to be evaluated by the insurance market?
modules.subhead: Receive a confidential, industry-specific assessment of your renewal process, risk controls, claims practices, and underwriting story—before speaking with anyone.
modules.audience: CFOs, COOs, and owners unsure whether the company is presenting an accurate, differentiated risk story.

modules.name: Renewal Control Tower
modules.headline: Is your next renewal on a timeline, or on autopilot?
modules.subhead: A confidential check of your renewal runway, the data carriers will ask for, and the changes that need to be documented before submissions go out.
modules.audience: CFOs and risk managers facing a renewal within three to nine months.
modules.focusIntro: Timing, data, and the story carriers receive. These answers determine whether preparation starts early enough to matter.

modules.name: Hidden Risk Transfer Scan
modules.headline: Are your contracts actually transferring risk, or just describing it?
modules.subhead: A confidential scan of how signed contracts, insurance requirements, certificates, and subcontractor terms work together as one control system.
modules.audience: COOs and CFOs in construction, manufacturing, real estate, and logistics who rely on vendors and subcontractors.
modules.focusIntro: Requirements that are never verified, and certificates that are never matched to contracts, do not transfer risk when a loss occurs.

modules.name: Claims Friction Index
modules.headline: Are claims being managed, or just reported?
modules.subhead: A confidential look at reporting speed, open-claim cadence, return-to-work practices, and how corrective actions are tracked.
modules.audience: CFO, HR, and operations leaders frustrated by recurring or poorly managed claims.
modules.focusIntro: Late reporting, unreviewed reserves, and untracked corrective actions are the most common reasons claims cost more and stay open longer.
